texts.exact_text: Pî indicates that there should be free course (in what it denotes). There will be little advantage (however) if it be allowed to advance (and take the lead).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first NINE, undivided, shows one adorning (the way of) his feet. He can discard a carriage and walk on foot.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second SIX, divided, shows one adorning his beard.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject with the appearance of being adorned and bedewed (with rich favours). But let him ever maintain his firm correctness, and there will be good fortune.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth SIX, divided, shows one looking as if adorned, but only in white. As if (mounted on) a white horse, and furnished with wings, (he seeks union with the subject of the first line), while (the intervening third pursues), not as a robber, but intent on a matrimonial alliance.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject adorned by (the occupants of) the heights and gardens. He bears his roll of silk, small and slight. He may appear stingy; but there will be good fortune in the end.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows one with white as his (only) ornament. There will be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, line 6

texts.exact_text:
The character Pî is the symbol of what is ornamental and of the act of adorning. As there is ornament in nature, so should there be in society; but its place is secondary to that of what is substantial. This is the view of king Wén in his Tuàn. The symbolism of the separate lines is sometimes fantastic.

Line 1 is strong, and in an odd place. It is at the very bottom of the hexagram, and is the first line of Lî, the trigram. for fire or light, and suggesting what is elegant and bright. Its subject has nothing to do but to attend to himself. Thus he cultivates -- adorns -- himself in his humble position; but if need be, righteousness requiring it, he can give up every luxury and indulgence.

Line 2 is weak and in its proper place, but with no proper correlate above. The strong line 3 is similarly situated. These two lines therefore keep together, and are as the beard and the chin. Line 1 follows 2. What is substantial commands and rules what is merely ornamental.

Line 3 is strong, and between two weak lines, which adorn it, and bestow their favours on it. But this happy condition is from the accident of place. The subject of the line must be always correct and firm to ensure its continuance.

Line 4 has its proper correlate in 1, from whose strength it should receive ornament, but 2 and the strong 3 intervene and keep them apart, so that the ornament is only white, and of no bright colour. Line 4, however, is faithful to 1, and earnest for their union. And finally line 3 appears in a good character, and not with the purpose to injure, so that the union of 1 and 4 takes place. All this is intended to indicate how ornament recognises the superiority of solidity. Compare the symbolism of the second line of Kun (No. 3), and that of the topmost line of Khwei (No. 38).

Line 5 is in the place of honour, and has no proper correlate in 2. It therefore associates with the strong 6, which is symbolised by the heights and gardens round a city, and serving both to protect and to beautify it. Thus the subject of the line receives adorning from without, and does not of itself try to manifest it. Moreover, in his weakness, his offerings of ceremony are poor and mean. But, as Confucius said, 'In ceremonies it is better to be sparing than extravagant.' Hence that stinginess does not prevent a good auspice.

Line 6 is at the top of the hexagram ䷕. Ornament has had its course, and here there is a return to pure, white, simplicity. Substantiality is better than ornament. 贲 ䷕
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 22; scan-backed transcription p. 103, notes

texts.exact_text: 賁：亨。小利有攸往。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 賁，亨；柔來而文剛，故亨。分剛上而文柔，故小利有攸往。剛柔交錯，天文也；文明以止，人文也。觀乎天文，以察時變；觀乎人文，以化成天下。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 彖

texts.exact_text: 山下有火，賁；君子以明庶政，无敢折獄。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初九：賁其趾，舍車而徒。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 舍車而徒，義弗乘也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 六二：賁其須。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 賁其須，與上興也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 九三：賁如濡如，永貞吉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 永貞之吉，終莫之陵也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 六四：賁如皤如，白馬翰如，匪寇婚媾。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 六四，當位疑也。匪寇婚媾，終无尤也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 六五：賁於丘園，束帛戔戔，吝，終吉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 六五之吉，有喜也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上九：白賁，无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 白賁无咎，上得志也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/賁; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 22, 小象 6

texts.exact_text:
(When it is said that) Pî indicates that there should be free course (in what it denotes):

(We see) the weak line coming and ornamenting the strong lines (of the lower trigram ☲), and hence (it is said that ornament) 'should have free course.' On the other hand, the strong line above ornaments the weak ones (of the upper trigram ☶), and hence (it is said) that 'there will be little advantage, if (ornament) be allowed to advance (and take the lead).' (This is illustrated in the) appearances that ornament the sky.

Elegance and intelligence (denoted by the lower trigram ☲) regulated by the arrest (denoted by the upper) suggest the observances that adorn human (society).

We look at the ornamental figures of the sky, and thereby ascertain the changes of the seasons. We look at the ornamental observances of society, and understand how the processes of transformation are accomplished all under heaven.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 22, p. 232

texts.exact_text: (The trigram ☶ representing) a mountain and ☲ that for fire under it form Pî. The superior man, in accordance with this, throws a brilliancy around his various processes of government, but does not dare (in a similar way) to decide cases of criminal litigation.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, p. 295

texts.exact_text: 'He can discard a carriage and walk on foot:' -- righteousness requires that he should not ride.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, line 1, p. 295

texts.exact_text: 'He adorns his beard:' -- he rouses himself to action (only) along with the (subject of the) line above.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, line 2, p. 295

texts.exact_text: 'The good fortune consequent on his ever maintaining firm correctness' is due to this,--that to the end no one will insult him.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, line 3, p. 295

texts.exact_text: 'The place occupied by the fourth six, (divided),' affords ground for doubt (as to its subject); but '(as the subject of the third pursues) not as a robber, but as intent on a matrimonial alliance,' he will in the end have no grudge against him.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, line 4, p. 295

texts.exact_text: 'The good fortune falling to the fifth six, (divided); affords occasion for joy.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, line 5, p. 295

texts.exact_text: 'The freedom from error attached to (the subject of) the topmost line, with no ornament but the (simple white),' shows how he has attained his aim.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 22, line 6, p. 295
